takeaways: Every case mixed 5-6 subjects; none was pure FR or pure tax. Choose cases by where the 15 descriptive marks sit, not by the story.

Most descriptives were Study Material illustrations with new figures: throughput TA ratio, swap ratio, EAC of machines, EMA, Ind AS 115 catch-up, PGBP computation. Find the illustration and swap the numbers.

MCQs turned on one word in the facts: 'inter-state' (IGST penalty = CGST + SGST), 'seating capacity 16' (ITC allowed), 'donated' (ITC blocked), 'related parties' (no CoC vote), 'associate' (s.185 exemption lost).
Cases 2 and 4 were the easiest marks; Case 3's 5-year Ind AS 115 table was the time trap. Picking the right 4 cases in the first 15 minutes decided the score.
Some rules here have changed since May 2024 (GST Tribunal pre-deposit, s.17(5)(i), updated-return window). Use the Nov 2026 Study Material figures, not this paper's.

questions.subject: IDT
questions.chapter: Offences and Penalties (CGST Act) read with s.20 IGST Act
questions.topic: Penalty for aiding or abetting an offence - s.122(3); IGST penalty = CGST + SGST penalty
questions.ask: Maximum penalty on the GST consultant firm that abetted filing of a return with false ITC figures on inter-state inward supplies.

options.a: No penalty is leviable on CA firm
options.c: Rs 25,000 under CGST and Rs 25,000 under SGST/UTGST
options.d: Rs 50,000 under CGST and Rs 50,000 under SGST/UTGST

questions.clue: 'charge of abetment and aiding for filing false return' + 'inter-state transactions'
think: Abetting = penalty on a third person, not the taxpayer's own penalty -> CGST s.122(3), up to Rs 25,000.
Twist word 'inter-state' -> the tax is IGST. IGST has no penalty table of its own; s.20 IGST borrows the CGST provisions and adds up the CGST and SGST penalties.
Chapter clear -> IDT index -> Offences and Penalties -> 'aids or abets'; then IGST s.20 proviso.
Rs 25,000 + Rs 25,000 = Rs 50,000, levied under IGST -> (b).

look_up.where: ICAI SM IDT - Offences and Penalties (s.122(3)); IGST Act s.20

questions.solve: S.122(3)(a) CGST: any person who aids or abets an offence listed in s.122(1) is liable to a penalty up to Rs 25,000; the SGST Act has the same Rs 25,000. The false ITC relates to inter-state supplies, so the tax involved is IGST. S.20 IGST applies the CGST provisions, and its proviso says the IGST penalty is the total of the CGST and SGST penalties: Rs 25,000 + Rs 25,000 = Rs 50,000 under IGST.
questions.answer: (b) Rs 50,000 under IGST
questions.trap: Picking (c): splitting into CGST + SGST is right only for intra-state supplies; for inter-state it is one IGST penalty of Rs 50,000.

questions.chapter: Profits and Gains of Business or Profession - Depreciation (s.32)
questions.topic: Normal depreciation, half-rate for use under 180 days, additional depreciation s.32(1)(iia); asset not used for business gets nothing
questions.ask: Total normal + additional depreciation for FY 2023-24 on the two vans and the forklift.
questions.clue: 'used one passenger vehicle (van) from 1st December 2023' + 'donated another passenger vehicle'
think: Depreciation + additional depreciation -> PGBP, s.32(1)(ii) and s.32(1)(iia). Chapter clear.
Filter the assets: donated van is not used for business -> no depreciation. Van used from 1 Dec 2023 -> used under 180 days -> half rate. Forklift from 5 July 2023 -> full rate.
Additional depreciation 20% is for new plant of a manufacturer but not for road transport vehicles -> forklift (works inside the factory) yes, van no.
Cost excludes GST because ITC is available on both (link it with 1.4).

look_up.where: ICAI SM DT - PGBP (Depreciation u/s 32)

Van in use: cost Rs 25,00,000 (GST not added - ITC available). Rate 15%; put to use 1.12.2023, i.e. under 180 days -> 7.5% = Rs 1,87,500. No additional depreciation (road transport vehicle is excluded from s.32(1)(iia)).
Donated van: not used for business -> nil.
Forklift: cost Rs 20,00,000 (GST not added - ITC available); used over 180 days. Normal 15% = Rs 3,00,000; additional 20% = Rs 4,00,000 (new machinery of a manufacturer, used inside the factory).

questions.subject: FR
questions.chapter: Ind AS 8 Accounting Policies, Changes in Accounting Estimates and Errors (with Ind AS 2 Inventories)
questions.topic: Change in cost formula (FIFO / weighted average) is a change in accounting policy
questions.ask: How to classify KLM's change in its inventory cost formula.

options.c: Neither a change in accounting estimate nor a change in accounting policy
options.d: Change in method of accounting

questions.clue: 'changed its inventory cost formula'
think: 'Cost formula' = FIFO or weighted average under Ind AS 2 -> a basis of measurement -> accounting policy.
Know it without the book: estimates are judgements of amounts (obsolescence, NRV, useful life); a formula or basis is a policy.
The Rs 50 lakh understatement is a distractor - it is the effect of the change, not an error.

questions.subject: FR
questions.chapter: Ind AS 40 Investment Property (with Ind AS 16 and Ind AS 8)
questions.topic: Transfer from owner-occupied PPE to investment property on change in use; not a change in accounting policy (Ind AS 8 para 16(a))
questions.ask: Should MNO reclassify the Mumbai building, leased out from April 2023, from PPE to investment property, and is that a change in accounting policy?
questions.clue: 'leased out the building located at Mumbai to a third party'
think: Building moved from own office to earning rent -> PPE (Ind AS 16) vs investment property (Ind AS 40); 'change in accounting policy?' -> Ind AS 8.
Chapter clear -> FR index -> Ind AS 40 -> 'transfers' / 'change in use'; Ind AS 8 -> para 16(a) 'differ in substance'.
Apply: end of owner-occupation = evidence of change in use -> transfer to investment property at carrying amount (cost model in India).
Then Ind AS 8: new facts, not a new policy -> prospective, no restatement.

look_up.where: ICAI SM FR - Ind AS 40 Investment Property; Ind AS 8
index_keywords: not a change in accounting policy

questions.solve:
Ind AS 16: PPE = tangible items held for use in production or supply, for rental to others or for administration, and used over more than one period.
Ind AS 40: investment property = land or building held to earn rentals or for capital appreciation, not for own use or for sale in the ordinary course.
Ind AS 40 para 57: transfer to or from investment property only when there is a change in use, e.g. end of owner-occupation. Transfer is at carrying amount (cost model) - no gain or loss.
Ind AS 8 para 16(a): applying a policy to transactions or events that differ in substance from earlier ones is not a change in accounting policy.
Facts: up to 31.3.2023 the building was MNO's office -> PPE. From April 2023 MNO moved to Thane and let the Mumbai building to a third party -> owner-occupation ended -> it now meets the investment property definition.
questions.answer:
Provisions
1. Ind AS 16: PPE is held for own use - production, supply of goods/services or administration.
2. Ind AS 40: investment property is held to earn rentals or capital appreciation, not for own use or sale.
3. Ind AS 40 para 57: a transfer is made only on a change in use, e.g. end of owner-occupation.
4. Ind AS 8 para 16(a): applying a policy to events that differ in substance from earlier events is not a change in accounting policy.
Analysis
Classification depends on why the entity holds the building. Up to 31.3.2023 MNO used it as its own office -> PPE. In April 2023 MNO shifted to its own building at Thane and let the Mumbai building to a third party. Owner-occupation has ended and the building is now held to earn rent - a real change in use.
Conclusion
(a) Yes. MNO should reclassify the Mumbai building from PPE to investment property from April 2023, at its carrying amount on that date (cost model under Ind AS 40), and disclose its fair value.
(b) No. This is not a change in accounting policy; it follows from a change in use (new facts). No retrospective restatement - the 31.3.2023 comparative stays as PPE.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI (reclassify; not a change in accounting policy). Added the Ind AS 40 para 57 transfer rule and carrying-amount measurement.
questions.trap: Treating the reclassification as a voluntary change in accounting policy and restating 2022-23.

questions.subject: Audit
questions.chapter: Audit Reports - SA 706 Emphasis of Matter, SA 705 Modified Opinion (with SA 580 Written Representations)
questions.topic: EOM cannot replace audit evidence; written representations alone are not sufficient
questions.ask: Is Mittal & Co. right to put the Rs 200 crore arbitration receivables in an Emphasis of Matter paragraph, based only on management's representation?
questions.clue: 'The audit firm Mittal & Co. has relied on management representation'
think: 'Emphasis of Matter' in the question -> SA 706; 'relied on management representation' -> SA 580 red flag.
Chapter clear -> Audit index -> SA 706 conditions: matter properly disclosed + fundamental to users + no modification needed under SA 705.
Ask: has the auditor earned the right to say 'no modification needed'? Only written representations -> no evidence -> he cannot.
Write: provision, procedures he skipped (contracts, arbitration status, legal counsel - SA 501), conclusion: EOM not proper now.

look_up.where: ICAI SM Audit - SA 706 / SA 705 (Audit Reports); SA 580

questions.solve: SA 706: an EOM paragraph points users to a matter already properly presented or disclosed in the FS that is fundamental to their understanding; it is used only when the auditor is not required to modify the opinion on that matter under SA 705. SA 580: written representations do not, on their own, give sufficient appropriate evidence. Facts: Rs 200 crore claims are disputed by clients and under arbitration; the auditor did no procedures beyond taking management's word.
questions.answer:
Provisions
- SA 706: an EOM paragraph draws attention to a matter that is appropriately presented or disclosed in the FS and is fundamental to users' understanding. It can be used only if the auditor is not required to modify the opinion on that matter under SA 705.
- SA 580: written representations do not by themselves provide sufficient appropriate audit evidence.
- SA 500/501: the auditor must obtain evidence, including on litigation and claims.
Analysis
- Rs 200 crore non-current receivables are cost-overrun claims that clients have not accepted; recovery depends on arbitration.
- Mittal & Co. relied only on management's representation. It did not examine the contracts and change orders, the arbitration status, legal counsel's view or past outcomes of similar claims.
- Without this evidence it cannot say whether the receivables are fairly stated. If they are materially overstated -> qualified/adverse opinion; if evidence cannot be obtained -> qualified opinion or disclaimer.
- An EOM paragraph is not a substitute for a modified opinion.
Conclusion
The EOM disclosure is not proper. Mittal & Co. should first perform these procedures. Only if it concludes that no modification is needed under SA 705, and the uncertainty is adequately disclosed in the FS, may it add an EOM paragraph on the arbitration.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI (not proper; obtain evidence first, EOM only if no modification is needed under SA 705).
questions.trap: Writing 'EOM is fine because the matter is material and uncertain' - EOM never cures missing audit evidence.

Throughput per unit (Rs) | 50 | 40 | 45

questions.subject: AFM
questions.chapter: Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management
questions.topic: Hedging policy steps and choice of instrument (forwards, futures, options, swaps, zero-cost collar)
questions.ask: Broad procedure to decide whether to hedge MAPL's forex risk and how to choose hedge instruments.
questions.clue: 'both interest risks and currency risk is taken care of' + 'zero cost hedge'
think: 'Whether to hedge' + 'which instruments' -> AFM Forex Risk Management - hedging policy and instruments.
Chapter clear -> AFM index -> 'hedging', 'currency swap', 'currency options', 'collar'.
Two parts score marks: the generic steps + mapping each exposure in the case to an instrument (JPY loan -> currency + interest swap; 40% of exports with upside -> options; zero-cost part -> collar).
Theory answer - write as steps; 15 minutes.

look_up.where: ICAI SM AFM - Foreign Exchange Exposure and Risk Management

questions.solve: Exposures in the case: (1) JPY 50 billion loan, 10 years, unhedged - both currency and interest risk; loan covenants were breached last year. (2) Export receivables - 40% to be hedged keeping the upside, part of it at zero cost. Build the answer as steps, then map instruments to these exposures.
questions.answer:
Broad procedure
Step 1 - Identify and measure exposures: JPY loan principal and interest, and export receivables; note the covenant breach last year.
Step 2 - Forecast exchange-rate (and interest-rate) movements and the chance of adverse moves, in-house or through forex forecasters.
Step 3 - Assess the impact on profit, cash flow, balance sheet and loan covenants under different scenarios.
Step 4 - Fix the hedging approach (conservative, dynamic/selective, or mixed) and decide how much to hedge within risk limits and covenant headroom - here 40% of exports.
Step 5 - Select instruments to fit each exposure: forwards for date-certain flows, futures where timing may not match, options where upside must be kept, swaps for long-term loans, zero-cost collars where no premium is wanted. Monitor and review the hedges.
Applied to MAPL
- JPY loan (currency + interest risk, 10 years): cross-currency interest rate swap (CIRCUS / currency coupon swap) converting JPY principal and interest into INR.
- 40% of exports with upside retained: buy currency options (put on the foreign currency).
- Zero-cost portion within that 40%: zero-cost collar - buy a put on the foreign currency (floor) and sell a call (cap) so the premiums offset; upside is kept up to the cap.
questions.icai: Same 5-step approach and instrument choice as ICAI (CIRCUS / currency coupon swap for the JPY loan; collar for the zero-cost part).

questions.subject: Law
questions.chapter: Companies Act 2013 - s.138 Internal Audit, Rule 13 Companies (Accounts) Rules 2014
questions.topic: Thresholds for compulsory internal audit and who can be internal auditor
questions.ask: When must a company appoint an internal auditor, who can be appointed, and from which year must MAPL have one?
questions.clue: 'company was having turnover of Rs 250 Crores in financial year 2022-23'
think: 'Required to have an internal auditor' -> Companies Act s.138 + Rule 13 thresholds (also covered under internal audit in Audit).
Chapter clear -> A-Z index 'internal audit' / 's.138' -> Rule 13 table.
Test the preceding year: FY 2022-23 turnover Rs 250 crore >= Rs 200 crore -> required for FY 2023-24 (the Rs 75 crore borrowing alone would not trigger it).
Extra marks: a special review of controls is not a substitute; the statutory auditor cannot be internal auditor (s.144).

look_up.where: Companies Act s.138 + Rule 13 (Inter Corporate Laws - Accounts of Companies; Audit SM - internal audit)

questions.solve: Rule 13 test for an unlisted public company (preceding FY): paid-up capital >= Rs 50 crore, or turnover >= Rs 200 crore, or bank/PFI borrowings >= Rs 100 crore at any time, or deposits >= Rs 25 crore at any time. MAPL: turnover FY 2022-23 Rs 250 crore -> condition met -> internal audit from FY 2023-24.
questions.answer:
When required [s.138 read with Rule 13, Companies (Accounts) Rules 2014]
(a) Every listed company.
(b) Every unlisted public company having, in the preceding FY: paid-up capital of Rs 50 crore or more; or turnover of Rs 200 crore or more; or outstanding loans/borrowings from banks or PFIs of Rs 100 crore or more at any time; or outstanding deposits of Rs 25 crore or more at any time.
(c) Every private company having, in the preceding FY: turnover of Rs 200 crore or more; or outstanding loans/borrowings from banks or PFIs of Rs 100 crore or more at any time.
Who can be appointed
- A chartered accountant or a cost accountant (in practice or not), or any other professional decided by the Board; may be an individual, a firm or a body corporate; may or may not be an employee.
- Appointed by Board resolution at a meeting [s.179(3)]; the Audit Committee/Board fixes scope, periodicity and methodology in consultation with the internal auditor.
- The statutory auditor cannot act as internal auditor [s.144].
MAPL
- Turnover in FY 2022-23 = Rs 250 crore, above Rs 200 crore -> MAPL must have an internal auditor from FY 2023-24. (Borrowing of Rs 75 crore is below Rs 100 crore and alone would not trigger it.)
- A special review of internal controls by AB & Co. does not replace internal audit under s.138.
- MAPL is already late for FY 2023-24 and should appoint one at once; AB & Co. can itself be appointed if it is not the statutory auditor.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI (required from FY 2023-24; CA/CMA or other professional). Added s.179(3), s.144 and the 'special review is not enough' point.
questions.trap: Testing the current year's figures - Rule 13 looks at the preceding financial year.

questions.subject: Audit
questions.chapter: SA 265 Communicating Deficiencies in Internal Control (with SA 610, SA 240, SA 330)
questions.topic: Statutory auditor's response to internal auditor's findings on receivable controls left unremedied
questions.ask: How should CA. R, the statutory auditor, respond to the internal auditor's findings on receivables controls that management has not fixed?
questions.clue: 'receivables not reconciled at regular intervals' + 'not taken any action on the deficiencies'
think: 'Deficiencies in internal control' raised by the internal auditor -> SA 610 (using internal audit findings) + SA 265 (communication).
'Management has also not taken any action' -> SA 240 fraud risk factor: failure to remedy known significant deficiencies.
Chapter clear -> Audit index -> SA 265 'significant deficiency'; SA 240 appendix 'fraud risk factors'.
Answer flow: assess -> communicate in writing -> extend substantive work on receivables -> report (SA 705 / IFC).

look_up.where: ICAI SM Audit - SA 265; SA 240; SA 610; SA 330

questions.solve: Two deficiencies: (1) no quarterly reconciliation of receivables; (2) credit limits never reviewed. Management ignored the internal auditor. Link: SA 610 (consider the findings) -> SA 240 (unremedied known deficiency = fraud risk factor) -> SA 265 (written communication of significant deficiencies) -> SA 330/505 (more substantive work) -> SA 705 / s.143(3)(i) (reporting).
questions.answer:
1. Consider the findings (SA 610 / SA 315): read the internal audit report and use the findings to assess the risk of material misstatement in trade receivables.
2. Fraud risk (SA 240): management's failure to remedy known significant deficiencies in time is a fraud risk factor (attitude/rationalisation). Unreconciled receivables and unchecked credit limits leave room for intentional misstatement - fictitious or overstated debtors, teeming and lading.
3. Evaluate and communicate (SA 265): decide whether the two deficiencies, alone or together, are significant - here they likely are. Communicate significant deficiencies in writing to those charged with governance (audit committee) and to management in time, and follow up on corrective action.
4. Respond in the audit (SA 330): do not rely on these controls; extend substantive procedures - external confirmation of balances (SA 505), year-end reconciliation of debtors' ledger with the control account, ageing analysis, subsequent receipts, review of sales beyond credit limits, adequacy of loss allowance.
5. Report: a letter of weakness does not reduce his reporting duty. If receivables remain materially misstated or evidence is insufficient, modify the opinion under SA 705; where IFC reporting applies [s.143(3)(i)], report the material weakness in internal financial controls over receivables.
Conclusion: CA. R should treat the findings as a fraud-risk indicator, communicate them in writing to the audit committee and management, extend substantive testing, and modify his report if the deficiencies result in material misstatement.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI (fraud risk factor; communicate via letter of weakness under SA 265; SA 705 if the deficiency persists). Added SA 330/505 procedures and IFC reporting.
questions.trap: Stopping at 'send a management letter' - the letter does not discharge the auditor's own reporting duty.

questions.subject: DT
questions.chapter: Appeals and Revision - s.254(2) rectification by ITAT
questions.topic: 6-month limit applies to filing the application; an application filed in time can be decided later (Sree Ayyanar Spinning & Weaving Mills, SC)
questions.ask: Can ITAT pass a s.254(2) rectification order beyond 6 months when the department applied late, and when can ITAT rectify after 6 months?
questions.clue: 'rectification order under section 254' + 'beyond 6 months from the end of the month'
think: 'Rectification order u/s 254' -> ITAT powers in Appeals and Revision; 6-month limit since Finance Act 2021.
Chapter clear -> DT index -> Appeals and Revision -> s.254(2); case-law list -> Sree Ayyanar Spinning (SC).
Separate two dates: when the application is filed (must be within 6 months) vs when ITAT decides (can be later).
Here the department filed late -> not maintainable -> ITAT cannot rectify.

look_up.where: ICAI SM DT - Appeals and Revision (s.254)

questions.solve: S.254(2): ITAT may amend its order to rectify a mistake apparent from record within 6 months from the end of the month in which the order was passed, and must do so if the assessee or AO brings the mistake to its notice. SC in Sree Ayyanar Spinning & Weaving Mills: an application filed within the limit must be decided on merits even after the limit. Facts: department applied after 6 months -> application time-barred.
questions.answer:
Provision
S.254(2): the ITAT may, within 6 months from the end of the month in which its order was passed, amend the order to rectify any mistake apparent from record. It must do so if the mistake is brought to its notice by the assessee or the Assessing Officer.
Judicial view
Sree Ayyanar Spinning & Weaving Mills Ltd. v. CIT (SC): the time limit governs the filing of the application. If the application is made within the limit, the Tribunal must decide it on merits even if its order comes after the limit; it cannot reject it on limitation.
Analysis
The department moved the application after 6 months from the end of the month of the ITAT order. A belated application is not maintainable, so the ITAT has no power to pass a rectification order on it.
When ITAT can rectify after 6 months
Only when the rectification application by the assessee or the AO is filed within 6 months from the end of the month of the original order. The ITAT is then bound to decide it on merits, even after the 6 months.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI (application not maintainable; order after 6 months only on an application filed in time).
questions.trap: Saying ITAT can never pass an order after 6 months - it can, if the application itself was filed in time.

questions.answer:
Provision
Under the provisos to s.2(15), 'advancement of any other object of general public utility' remains a charitable purpose only if any trade, commerce or business activity is carried on in the course of actually carrying out that object and the aggregate receipts from it do not exceed 20% of the institution's total receipts for the year. If the limit is crossed, s.13(8) denies exemption u/s 11/12 for that year.
Analysis
Total receipts Rs 150 lakh; 20% = Rs 30 lakh. Receipts from the trade-like activity Rs 32 lakh > Rs 30 lakh.
Advice
- Swayam is not 'charitable' for PY 2023-24 and loses the exemption u/s 11 for that year; its income is taxable (s.13(10) allows revenue expenditure incurred in India on its objects while computing that income).
- Applying 85% of the receipts to its object does not save the exemption.
- Registration/approval is not automatically cancelled; the exemption can be claimed again in a later year if trade receipts stay within 20%.

questions.trap: Thinking that spending 85% of the receipts on the object saves the exemption - the 20% receipts test is separate from application.

questions.solve: Kaizen costing is a cost reduction tool: it sets cost reduction targets and assumes continuous improvement of processes, with targets set and reviewed over short periods (usually monthly). questions.chapter: Registration - non-resident taxable person (s.2(77), s.24, s.27; Rule 13)
questions.topic: NRTP: compulsory registration, passport-based application, advance tax deposit, 90-day validity
questions.ask: Is Mano a non-resident taxable person under CGST, and if so what must he comply with? (Part of a 6-mark question; mark split assumed.)
questions.clue: 'came to India on 2nd January 2024 to render his expert service'
think: 'Non-resident taxable person' is named in the question -> GST Registration: s.2(77), s.24, s.27, Rule 13.
Chapter clear -> IDT index -> Registration -> special provisions for casual and non-resident taxable persons.
Fit the facts: occasional supply of services, no fixed place of business or residence in India -> NRTP.
List the procedure as points: compulsory registration, 5 days before, passport-based REG-09, advance deposit, 90-day validity + extension, no composition.

look_up.where: ICAI SM IDT - Registration (casual and non-resident taxable persons)

questions.solve: S.2(77): NRTP = person who occasionally undertakes transactions involving supply of goods/services but has no fixed place of business or residence in India. Mano: short visit, supplies expert services to Magic Ltd., no fixed place of business or residence in India -> NRTP -> s.24 compulsory registration + s.27 special rules.
questions.answer:
Definition: s.2(77) - a non-resident taxable person (NRTP) occasionally undertakes transactions involving supply of goods or services, as principal, agent or otherwise, but has no fixed place of business or residence in India.
Mano: he came for a short assignment, supplies expert services to Magic Ltd. and has no fixed place of business or residence in India -> he is an NRTP.
Procedure
(a) Compulsory registration u/s 24, whatever the turnover; apply at least 5 days before starting business.
(b) Apply in Form GST REG-09 with a self-attested copy of his valid passport (no Indian PAN needed), signed or e-verified by his authorised signatory in India who has a valid PAN; his foreign tax identification number may be given.
(c) Pay an advance deposit of tax equal to the estimated tax liability for the period of registration; it is credited to his electronic cash ledger.
(d) Registration is valid for the period stated in the application or 90 days from the effective date, whichever is earlier; extendable by up to 90 days on request with a further advance deposit.
(e) He cannot opt for the composition levy.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI (NRTP; registration procedure).
questions.flag: Arguable view: Mano has no establishment in India, so as supplier he is located outside India and his service to Magic Ltd. could be an import taxed under RCM in Magic's hands (Notification 10/2017-IT(R)); ICAI treats him as an NRTP who must register.
questions.trap: Applying the Rs 20 lakh threshold - an NRTP must register regardless of turnover.

questions.ask: Is Mano's Rs 50 lakh taxable in India, at what rate, and how much tax must Magic Ltd. deduct when it bears the tax? (Part of a 6-mark question; mark split assumed.)
questions.clue: 'Magic Ltd. had agreed with Mano to bear the tax liability'
think: Four steps in order: residence (s.6) -> taxability (s.9(1)(vii) FTS) -> rate (s.115A) -> TDS with grossing up (s.195A).
Days: 2 Jan - 25 Mar 2024 = 30 + 29 + 25 = 84 days (below 120 and 182) -> non-resident for PY 2023-24.
Expert mechanical engineering service = technical/consultancy -> FTS; agreement under Industrial Policy -> 20% u/s 115A + surcharge 10% (income above Rs 50 lakh) + cess 4% = 22.88%.

Residential status: Mano, a person of Indian origin coming on a visit, is resident only if in India for 182 days or more (or, if his Indian income exceeds Rs 15 lakh, 120 days in the PY plus 365 days in the preceding 4 years). He stayed 84 days (2.1.2024 to 25.3.2024) -> non-resident for AY 2024-25. (Deemed residence u/s 6(1A) applies only to Indian citizens.)

questions.subject: Law
questions.chapter: Meetings of Board and its Powers - s.185 Loans to directors (exemption notification for private companies)
questions.topic: Private company exemption fails when a body corporate has invested in its share capital; penalties u/s 185(4)
questions.ask: Consequences under the Companies Act of Lion Pvt. Ltd.'s Rs 25 lakh loan to its director Santosh.
questions.clue: 'Lion Private Limited- an associate of Magic Limited' + 'advanced Rs 25 lakhs to its director'
think: 'Loan to director' + 'Companies Act' -> s.185 and the 2015/2017 exemption for private companies.
Chapter clear -> SPOM Set A / Law index -> s.185 -> exemption to private companies: 3 conditions.
Key word 'associate of Magic Limited' -> a body corporate holds its shares -> condition (a) fails -> no exemption.
Then s.185(4) penalties on the company, officers in default and the director who took the loan.

look_up.where: SPOM Set A (Corporate & Economic Laws) - Meetings of Board and its Powers (s.185)

questions.solve: S.185(1) bars loans to directors. Private-company exemption needs: (a) no body corporate invested in its share capital; (b) borrowings from banks/FIs/bodies corporate below 2x paid-up capital or Rs 50 crore, whichever is lower; (c) no default in repaying such borrowings. Lion is an associate of Magic Ltd. -> Magic has invested -> (a) fails -> s.185 applies -> loan contravenes s.185(1) -> s.185(4) penalties.
questions.answer:
Provision: s.185(1) - a company shall not, directly or indirectly, give a loan (including book debt), or a guarantee or security for a loan, to any of its directors or a director of its holding company, any partner or relative of such director, or any firm in which such director or relative is a partner (subject to s.185(3) exceptions, e.g. loan to an MD/WTD as part of service conditions or an approved scheme).
Private company exemption (MCA notification of 5.6.2015, amended 13.6.2017): s.185 does not apply to a private company (a) in whose share capital no other body corporate has invested; (b) whose borrowings from banks, FIs or bodies corporate are less than twice its paid-up capital or Rs 50 crore, whichever is lower; and (c) which is not in default in repaying such borrowings at the time of the transaction.
Analysis: Lion Pvt. Ltd. is an associate of Magic Ltd., so Magic Ltd., a body corporate, has invested in its share capital -> condition (a) fails and the exemption is lost. Conditions (b) and (c) appear met (no contrary facts), and Santosh's 25% holding does not affect the exemption. Santosh is a director, the loan is for his house, and no s.185(3) exception applies. The Rs 25 lakh loan therefore contravenes s.185(1).
Consequences [s.185(4)]:
(i) Company - fine of Rs 5 lakh to Rs 25 lakh.
(ii) Every officer in default - imprisonment up to 6 months or fine of Rs 5 lakh to Rs 25 lakh.
(iii) Santosh, the director who took the loan - imprisonment up to 6 months or fine of Rs 5 lakh to Rs 25 lakh, or both.
questions.icai: Same conclusion as ICAI (exemption fails on condition (a); s.185(4) penalties apply).
questions.trap: Assuming every private company is exempt from s.185 - the word 'associate' means a body corporate has invested, which kills the exemption.
